Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Ethnic/Geographic Tension: Arab villages, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Stress: Stress
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied, Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Vignette:
Clara had been stationed in a rural research outpost when the fire broke out at the neighboring processing facility. She watched from the observation deck as the flames swallowed the storage units, the crackle of burning timber and the sharp hiss of collapsing pipes echoing in her ears. She remembers the sudden stress of the evacuation sirens and the weight of watching a junior colleague stumble backward, unshielded, toward the thickening smoke. She had come to believe she should have protected others and she had failed, freezing in place while the heat rolled past the glass. Even now, she is certain that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation; the circumstances felt uniquely imposed on her, as though the odds had turned against her specifically. Over the following months, the event refused to settle into ordinary recollection. Her memories of the fire felt more real than normal, as vivid as if the heat were still pressing against her skin. The trauma of witnessing another’s peril left her hyper-vigilant to her surroundings. A sudden gust of wind carrying the scent of burnt paper could trigger her without warning, instantly pulling her back to the smoke-choked corridor. Sometimes, when the quiet of her apartment deepened, she would hear things in her head that she heard during the frightening event—the metallic groan of shifting steel, the urgent calls of her team—layering over the present without her choosing to summon them. She found herself checking doors and windows repeatedly, the ritual becoming automatic, a necessary bulwark against the unpredictability of the outside world. Strangers approaching her in the market or on the street felt suddenly threatening, their proximity reading like an intrusion, even in ordinary situations. Places holding similar architectural or cultural textures to the Arab villages she had traversed stirred the same familiar geographic and ethnic tension, her body bracing before her mind could catch up. To keep her mind occupied, Clara threw herself into her work or tasks, spending her days entangled in code and spreadsheets. She worked excessively to avoid being alone with her thoughts, extending her hours until the house emptied around her. Her home office, filled with dual monitors and stacks of printed reports, became both sanctuary and trap. During a late evening audit, she remembers staring at a cluster of red warning flags on a dashboard, the glowing embers on the screen mirroring the flames she had witnessed. The visual trigger was immediate; she felt the familiar surge of stress, her pulse quickening as she reached across the desk to verify that the patio door was latched, then checked it again. At the same time, she would go over and over why the event happened to her, caught in a quiet loop of self-comparison, wondering why she bore the weight while others carried on unharmed. The overwork and the rumination moved through her days side by side, neither erasing the other. Now, at forty, Clara sits in the quiet hours before dawn, her marriage steady but punctuated by the distance she maintains during the day. What finally brought her to seek help was a quiet afternoon when a visiting courier had stepped too close to examine a package, and the sudden flash of recognition had dropped her to her knees, her body acting as if the collapse were happening all over again. She is not sure her life is worth living anymore, a thought that settles heavily when the workday ends and the silence rushes in. She hopes for a way to untangle the past from the present, to let the memories soften without losing their meaning, and to walk through a room without bracing for another fire to begin.
